item.passage: Transcript: Vaissalu's drawings, set beside the stones that still stand. He drew some forty memorials in the seventeen nineties; nine of those stones survive. The comparison isn't flattering. The letterforms he gives are wrong in the same places an earlier antiquarian, Rennik, had gone wrong — same bind-runes, same swallowed vowel. He was copying Rennik's sketchbook, not the stone. Two things he's innocent of, mind: where a stone had flaked, he leaves a gap, honestly blank; and his churchyard attributions hold up wherever we can test them. How did I come to this? The parsonage at Kolgama. I catalogued its library as a student, one wet summer, and there was Rennik's sketchbook. That's the whole connection — no squeezes have ever come out of that house, the glebe wall there is nineteenth-century brick, and Kolgama's own pastors kept none of the visitation books that first mention the stones. The dating quarrel now. Hallik dates the group later than the years carved on it. I'd narrow that. One carver, the Ansu master, worked late, and his pieces colour how the rest get read; I would not extend that to the group. The formulas are common regional ones, older than any printed model I know, and the stone there weathers fast, so I don't rest a case on weathering. Twenty-odd stones are unlocated. We won't print a text nobody has seen on the stone, and they stay in the corpus volume, marked missing. A handlist goes to the county museums; some may sit unrecognized in a storeroom. The radio appeal was tried upriver and turned up little but field boulders.

It is a weather book as much as an instrument book, and that is why it earned its keep. A low background rumble sits on the Luhemaa traces that autumn, and the daily wind and sea entries let us set storm surf aside as its source — the rumble is loudest on flat, still days. The observer's felt account went to a newspaper the same week; the logbook closes in the same year the official history gives; and the crate surfaced through a museum's accession list, not through anything in the logbook. Tammik has argued for two ruptures minutes apart, and Oks thinks the magnitude drops once you model those old instruments. Neither holds: the trace shows one rupture, and the magnitude barely moves. The source sits under the coastal parish the catalogues name. What changes is the damage — the river towns stand on soft alluvium, and that, more than the size of the shock, drew the map of ruin. The sheets survive nearly complete. Hardly a sheet is missing from the years the network changed hands, the years before nineteen fifteen are as thickly covered as any, and each sheet carries its station's stamp. The trouble is framing: someone trimmed the margins off for display, and the time marks went with them. Kolmsaare? I am persuaded. The aftershocks sit along its mapped trend. The northern structure fits the uplift no better, these are not scattered shocks in healed crust, and the Kolmsaare structure is young.

item.prompt: [Academic Talk — Dance History] What is the professor's position on the claim that the roll records the ballet as it was first staged?
choices: She reads it as a teaching document, setting down what dancers were drilled on rather than any staging given

item.passage: Transcript: The Vantsi roll — nine metres of notation, and the question everyone asks first: which staging is this? My answer is the plain one. It is the first staging. Look at the ensemble figures: thirty-two dancers crammed into the downstage third, exactly the crowding the opening reviews complained of. The ensemble numbers here are not thinned, they are packed. Nor is this a drill book — the roll follows one evening's order straight through — and the entrances are in the same ink and the same hand as the figures, so nobody redrew them for a later season. What does it actually record? The corps, in detail. Their steps are written out in full, each number carried through to its end. The soloists get a line of description apiece, no more. And the mime scenes are passed over in a phrase, where later notations linger on them. Now the wrapper. There is a customs stamp on it, and three articles have built an itinerary out of that stamp. The stamp dates a crate of linen thread, not the roll's journey; the wrapper is freight paper somebody reused, and the address on it has sent people to the wrong city. Wrapper and roll are of a piece, the same decade, and the stamp is a western port's. Next? We are going to dance it. One suite, with students, in the spring — the performance is the test. The order of the numbers is not in doubt, so the orchestral parts can wait, the rubbed passages were already read under raking light last winter, and the ballroom manuals are somebody else's project.
